subject: chemistry
title: Structure and bonding of carbon
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Structure and bonding of carbon — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.2.3.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Structure and bonding of carbon, specification section 4.2.3.
final_note: You worked through Structure and bonding of carbon — 12 specification statements.

concepts.def: A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure. Diamond is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.

A structure in which a very large number of atoms are joined to their neighbours by strong covalent bonds that run right through the substance. There are no separate small molecules, so there are no weak forces between molecules to overcome.

Every carbon atom in diamond is joined to four others by strong covalent bonds, in a rigid three-dimensional network. No atom can be pushed out of position without breaking covalent bonds, so diamond is very hard.

concepts.term: Why diamond has a very high melting point
concepts.def: Diamond is a giant covalent structure, so melting it means breaking a very large number of strong covalent bonds. This takes a great deal of energy, so the melting point is very high.

concepts.term: Why diamond does not conduct electricity
concepts.def: Each carbon atom in diamond uses all four of its outer electrons to form covalent bonds. There are no delocalised electrons, so there is nothing free to move through the structure and carry charge.
A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings.

The hexagonal rings of graphite are joined into flat layers, and there are no covalent bonds between the layers. The layers are held to one another only by weak forces of attraction, so they can slide over each other.

In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised. Because each atom uses only three of its outer electrons in covalent bonds, the fourth is not held on one atom and is free to move through the structure, carrying charge and thermal energy.

concepts.term: Why graphite is soft and slippery
concepts.def: There are no covalent bonds between the layers of graphite, so whole layers can slide over one another. Layers rub off easily, which is why graphite leaves a mark on paper and can act as a lubricant.

One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised, so these electrons are free to move through the structure. Moving electrons carry charge, so graphite conducts electricity, and they also carry thermal energy.

concepts.term: Why graphite has a very high melting point
concepts.def: Within each layer the carbon atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds. A very large number of these strong bonds must be broken to melt graphite, so the melting point is very high even though graphite is soft.

concepts.term: How graphite is similar to a metal
concepts.def: Graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons. These delocalised electrons let graphite conduct electricity and thermal energy in the way that the delocalised electrons of a metal do, although graphite is a non-metal whose atoms are joined by covalent bonds.

A single layer of graphite: one sheet of carbon atoms, each joined to three others by covalent bonds in hexagonal rings, one atom thick. Graphene has properties that make it useful in electronics and composites.

Because graphene is a single layer of graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised, so graphene conducts electricity, which makes it useful in electronics. Every atom in the sheet is held by strong covalent bonds, so graphene is very strong for its mass, which makes it useful in composites.
A molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape. The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms.
The first fullerene to be discovered, C60, which has a spherical shape.

A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio, which means the tube is extremely long compared with how wide it is. Their properties make carbon nanotubes useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials.

Fullerenes are hollow, so other molecules can be held inside the cage, which is used to deliver drugs into the body. They have a large surface area, so they can be used as catalysts, and they are also used as lubricants. Carbon nanotubes are used in nanotechnology and electronics, and are added to materials to reinforce them, for example in tennis racket frames.

Graphene is drawn or described as a single flat sheet of hexagonal rings, one atom thick, with no layers above or below it. Fullerenes are drawn or described as closed hollow shapes, a ball or a tube, built mainly from hexagonal rings and sometimes containing rings of five or seven carbon atoms. Graphite is drawn as several such sheets stacked in layers.

mcqs.q: In diamond, how many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form, and with what?
options: Four covalent bonds, within a small carbon molecule
Four covalent bonds, with four other carbon atoms
Four covalent bonds, with atoms of other elements
Three covalent bonds, with three other carbons
mcqs.explain: The specification states that in diamond each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
options: The carbon atoms in diamond do not contain any electrons
Its molecules are packed too tightly for electrons to move
All four outer electrons of each carbon atom are held in bonds
The covalent bonds in diamond are far too strong to break
mcqs.explain: With every outer electron used in a covalent bond there are no delocalised electrons free to move and carry charge.

mcqs.q: Diamond has a very high melting point. What is the reason?
options: The weak forces between the diamond molecules must be overcome
A very large number of strong covalent bonds must be broken
Diamond has no free electrons to carry energy through it
The carbon atoms in diamond are unusually heavy atoms
mcqs.explain: Diamond is a giant covalent structure, so melting it means breaking huge numbers of strong covalent bonds.

mcqs.q: Which feature of diamond's structure explains why it is very hard?
options: The layers of carbon atoms are unable to slide past each other
There are no delocalised electrons anywhere in the structure
The carbon atoms are much smaller than the atoms of a metal
Every atom is held in place by four strong covalent bonds
mcqs.explain: The rigid three-dimensional network means no atom can move without covalent bonds being broken.

mcqs.q: In graphite, each carbon atom forms:
options: three covalent bonds, plus weak covalent bonds between layers
four covalent bonds, as in every other form of carbon
three covalent bonds, forming layers of hexagonal rings
two covalent bonds, forming long chains of carbon atoms
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's description of graphite: three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings.

mcqs.q: What lies between the layers of hexagonal rings in graphite?
options: No covalent bonds at all, only weak forces of attraction
Weak covalent bonds, which are broken easily by rubbing
The fourth outer electron of each atom, fixed in position
Covalent bonds that are weaker than the ones in diamond
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the layers have no covalent bonds between them, which is why they slide.

mcqs.q: In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is:
options: delocalised, and free to move through the structure
left on its own atom, in the outer shell where it began
used to bond weakly to the layer above and below
lost completely, leaving the carbon atom positively charged
mcqs.explain: The specification states that in graphite one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.

mcqs.q: Graphite is soft enough to leave a mark on paper. Why?
options: The covalent bonds within graphite are weak and break easily
Its delocalised electrons let the atoms slip past each other
Its layers can slide because no covalent bonds join them
It melts at a low temperature, so it wears away very easily
mcqs.explain: With no covalent bonds between the layers, whole layers slide over one another and rub off.

options: One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and moves
Its layers slide over each other and carry the charge
Each carbon atom holds a spare electron in its outer shell
It is a metal, and every metal conducts electricity well
mcqs.explain: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure, and moving electrons carry charge.

mcqs.q: Graphite is soft, yet its melting point is very high. Why?
options: Its melting point is in fact low, which is why it is soft
The covalent bonds within each layer are strong and numerous
The weak forces between layers must be broken to melt it
Its delocalised electrons carry heat out of the solid
mcqs.explain: Melting graphite means breaking a very large number of the strong covalent bonds inside the layers.

mcqs.q: In what way is graphite similar to a metal?
options: Graphite is a metal, so it behaves in the same way
Graphite is held together by metallic bonds as well
Graphite contains a small amount of metal in its layers
Graphite has delocalised electrons, as metals do
mcqs.explain: The specification states that graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons.

options: a hollow ball of carbon atoms, like a fullerene
a single layer of graphite, one atom thick
a stack of graphite layers, very thinly sliced
a compound of carbon with another element
mcqs.explain: The specification defines graphene as a single layer of graphite.

mcqs.q: Why is graphene useful in electronics and in composites?
options: It is one atom thick, so it bends and stretches very easily
It is hollow, so other substances can be held inside it
It is a metal, and metals conduct well and are very strong
It has delocalised electrons and strong covalent bonds
mcqs.explain: One delocalised electron per carbon atom lets it conduct, and the strong covalent bonds make it strong for its mass.

mcqs.q: Which statement about fullerenes is correct?
options: They are built from hexagonal rings of carbon and nothing else
They are all spheres containing exactly 60 carbon atoms
They are hollow molecules based on hexagonal rings of carbon
They are giant covalent structures like diamond and graphite
mcqs.explain: The specification describes fullerenes as molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes, based on hexagonal rings.

options: A cylinder with a very high length to diameter ratio
A sphere of 60 atoms, and the only shape a fullerene takes
A flat sheet of hexagonal rings, sixty carbon atoms across
The first fullerene discovered, C60, with a spherical shape
mcqs.explain: This is exactly what the specification states about Buckminsterfullerene.

mcqs.q: Which statement about carbon nanotubes is correct?
options: They are not fullerenes, because fullerenes are spherical
Their high length to diameter ratio makes them wide tubes
They are cylindrical fullerenes, very long and very thin
They are one atom thick, so they are weak and bend easily
mcqs.explain: The specification describes carbon nanotubes as cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios.

mcqs.q: A diagram shows a flat sheet of hexagonal carbon rings, one atom thick, with no layers above or below it. What does the diagram show?
options: A fullerene, because fullerenes are sheets of hexagons
Graphene, a single layer of graphite one atom thick
Graphite, because graphite is made of hexagonal rings
A nanotube, viewed from the side as a flattened sheet
mcqs.explain: A single layer of hexagonal rings with nothing above or below it is exactly graphene.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of a use of fullerenes?
options: Making thick cables that can be seen with the naked eye
Acting as a single flat sheet inside touchscreen glass
Burning in oxygen to release energy as a cheap fuel
Delivering drugs into the body inside their hollow cages
mcqs.explain: Fullerenes are hollow, so molecules can be held inside the cage and carried into the body.

mcqs.q: Carbon nanotubes are added to the frame of a tennis racket. Why?
options: They are very strong, so they reinforce the material used
They are thin, so they let the frame bend much more easily
They are wide tubes, so they fill the space inside the frame
They are soft and slippery, so they reduce friction in it
mcqs.explain: Their strength is why nanotubes are added to materials, one of the uses the specification names.
